extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in probabilistic graphical models, statistical mechanics, and descriptive complexity theory
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, properties, and correspondences between Markov random fields, Gibbs distributions, factor graphs, and directed graphical models; plus fixed‑point logics (LFP/IFP/PFP) and their connection to complexity classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation in graphs (Definition 2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A, B, C be three disjoint subsets of the vertices V of a graph G. The set C is said to separate A and B if every path from a vertex in A to a vertex in B must pass through C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to state global conditional independencies: if C separates A and B then one expects A ⟂⟂ B | C for distributions respecting the graph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Markov property (Definition 2.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The distribution Xi (for every i) is conditionally independent of the rest of the graph given just the variables that lie in the neighborhood of the vertex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: influence on a variable is completely described by its neighborhood variables alone; local conditional distributions are the 'local characteristics' of the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global Markov property (Definition 2.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any disjoint subsets A, B, C of V such that C separates A from B in the graph, it holds that A ⟂⟂ B | C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expresses conditional independencies implied by graph separation; relates to factorization properties of distributions that respect the graph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markov random field (Definition 2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection X1,...,Xn is a Markov random field wrt a neighborhood system on G iff (1) the distribution is positive on the space of configurations: P(x) > 0 for x ∈ Ωn, and (2) for each vertex, the distribution at that vertex is conditionally independent of all other vertices given just those in its neighborhood: P(Xi | X_{V\i}) = P(Xi | X_{Ni}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positivity + local conditional independence define the field; local conditionals (local characteristics) determine the joint when positivity holds [Bes74].

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity condition for MRFs
rubrics_metrics.description: The distribution must be positive on the space of configurations: P(x) > 0 for all x ∈ Ωn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This positivity is essential for full equivalence with Gibbs distributions (Hammersley–Clifford). Relaxing positivity can produce distributions with Markov properties that do not admit Gibbs factorization (see Example 2.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gibbs random field / Gibbs distribution (Definition 2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: A probability measure on Ωn having representation P(x) = (1/Z) exp(−U(x)/T), where Z is the partition function, T is temperature, and U(x) = ∑_{c∈C} V_c(x) is the energy expressed as a sum over clique potentials V_c that depend only on variables in clique c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gibbs form is a factorization into clique 'interaction potentials' and captures interactions via cliques. Partition function Z is global and generally intractable to evaluate exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition function, temperature, and clique potentials (components of Gibbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Z = ∑_{x∈Ωn} exp(−U(x)/T) is the normalizing partition function; T controls sharpness of distribution; U(x)=∑_{c∈C} V_c(x) with V_c depending only on coordinates in clique c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High T → near-uniform distribution; low T → mass on low-energy states. Evaluating Z is computationally hard due to summation over all configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a Gibbs distribution (Definition 2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Support of potential V_c is the cardinality of clique c. The degree deg(P) is the maximum support of the potentials — i.e., the size of the largest clique in the factorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree measures interaction complexity; larger degree implies more parameters and higher algorithmic hurdle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hammersley–Clifford theorem (Theorem 2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: X is a Markov random field wrt neighborhood system NG on graph G iff it is a Gibbs random field wrt the same neighborhood system (given the positivity condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes equivalence between local conditional independencies (Markov) and global Gibbs factorization under positivity; positivity is essential; historical remarks and references given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexample to Gibbs factorization without positivity (Example 2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructed distribution on four binary variables that satisfies the global Markov property wrt the 4-cycle but does not factorize into Gibbs potentials, illustrating the necessity of positivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: having Markov conditional independencies alone (without positivity) does not guarantee Gibbs factorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor graphs and factorization (Section 2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor graphs are bipartite graphs with variable nodes and factor nodes expressing decomposition of a global multivariate function into local functions; they represent factorization p(x)= (1/Z) ∏ ϕ_i(subset of variables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor graphs give a finer-grained factorization but do not in general imply conditional independence — the partition function carries global constraints. Useful in algorithmic contexts (belief propagation), especially on tree-like structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion of factor graphs and Gibbs property
rubrics_metrics.description: A clique in a factor graph is a set of variable nodes pairwise connected by a function node. The completion is obtained by adding a function node for each clique connected to its variables. A positive distribution satisfying the global Markov property wrt a factor graph satisfies the Gibbs property wrt its completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a Hammersley–Clifford type statement for factor graphs via their completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed graphical models / Bayesian networks factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: For a DAG, the joint distribution factors as p(x1,...,xn) = ∏_{n=1}^N p(x_n | x_{pa(n)}), where pa(n) are the parents of node n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directed factorizations are recursively normalized; they encode conditional independence (node independent of non-descendants given parents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moralization (conversion of DAG to undirected graph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moralization: (a) replace directed edges by undirected edges, and (b) 'marry' the parents of every vertex by adding edges between each pair of parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to obtain an undirected graph (the moral graph) whose cliques reflect conditional dependencies implied by the DAG; employed in proofs relating directed factorization to undirected potentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive factorization via kernels (Definition 2.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure p admits a recursive factorization according to graph G if there exist non-negative kernels k_v(y_v, x_{pa(v)}) normalized so that ∫ k_v(y_v,x_{pa(v)}) μ_v(dy_v) = 1 and p = f·μ where f(x)=∏_{v∈V} k_v(x_v,x_{pa(v)}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kernels are conditional densities of X_v given its parents; when such a recursive factorization exists, p admits a factorization into potentials according to the moral graph (Theorem 2.13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed-to-undirected factorization (Theorem 2.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p admits a recursive factorization according to G, then it admits a factorization (into potentials) according to the moral graph G^m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the connection between directed Bayesian network factorizations and undirected Gibbs factorizations via moralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: D-separation (directed models)
rubrics_metrics.description: A directed path from A to B is blocked by C if (1) arrows meet head-to-tail or tail-to-tail at a node in C, or (2) arrows meet head-to-head at a node and neither the node nor any of its descendants is in C. If all directed paths from A to B are blocked then C D-separates A from B, implying A ⟂⟂ B | C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: D-separation is the directed analogue of graph separation and gives the conditional independencies implied by a DAG.

rubrics_metrics.name: I-map, D-map, and P-map (Definitions 2.14–2.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: A graph is a D-map if every conditional independence satisfied by the distribution is reflected in the graph. A graph is an I-map if every conditional independence expressed by the graph is satisfied by the distribution. A P-map is both an I-map and D-map (perfect map), expressing exactly the conditional independencies of the distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trivial examples: completely disconnected graph is a D-map for any distribution; complete graph is a I-map for any distribution. Not all distributions have P-maps; directed P-maps differ from undirected P-maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametrization complexity (Section 2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: To specify joint distribution of n binary covariates without constraints requires 2^n − 1 parameters. Independence reduces this to n parameters. If factorization yields conditionally independent factors each of scope ≤ k, then specification needs O(n 2^k) parameters; directed models with at most k parents need at most n 2^k parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor graphs alone do not guarantee conditional independence, so one cannot infer parameter savings from factor graphs alone. Parametrization complexity captures the 'economy' of representing distributions and connects to algorithmic tractability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of irreducible interaction size and algorithmic implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of the smallest irreducible interactions (largest clique or minimal interactions that cannot be factored) determines the number of independent parameters: if smallest irreducible interactions are O(n) you need O(c^n) parameters; if interactions have scope poly(log n) you need O(c^{poly(log n)}) parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This measure is used to link factorization structure to whether problems lie in P (economical parametrization) versus requiring exponentially many parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operators on sets: monotone and inflationary (Definitions 3.1–3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operator F: P(A) → P(A) is monotone if X ⊆ Y ⇒ F(X) ⊆ F(Y). It is inflationary if X ⊆ F(X). The sequence F^0 = ∅, F^{i+1} = F(F^i) is inductive for monotone or inflationary F, and stabilizes to F^∞ = ⋃_i F^i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operator properties underlie inductive constructions and fixed point definitions used in logic (LFP/IFP/PFP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed points and least fixed point (Definition 3.4, Tarski–Knaster Theorem 3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: X is a fixed point of F if F(X)=X. The least fixed point LFP(F) is the intersection of all fixed points and equals the union of the stages of the F^i sequence when F is monotone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotonicity guarantees existence and constructibility of least fixed points; this is the foundation for FO(LFP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inflationary and partial fixed points (Definitions 3.6–3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: For arbitrary operator G, define Ginfl(Y)=Y ∪ G(Y); Ginfl^∞ is inflationary fixed point IFP(G). For an arbitrary operator F, partial fixed point PFP(F) is F^n if the sequence stabilizes, otherwise empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constructions allow fixed-point semantics for non-monotone operators (IFP, PFP) used in logic extensions; behavior differs from LFP (which requires monotonicity/positivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-point extensions of FO: FO(IFP), FO(PFP), FO(LFP) (Definitions 3.9, 3.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: FO(IFP): extend FO with [IFP_{R,x} φ](t) meaning a ∈ IFP(F_φ). FO(PFP): extend FO with [PFP_{R,x} φ](t) meaning a ∈ PFP(F_φ). FO(LFP): extend FO with [LFP_{R,x} φ](t) for φ positive in R, with semantics a ∈ LFP(F_φ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LFP requires positivity (no negative occurrences of R) to ensure monotonicity and decidable syntax; IFP/PFP allow broader operators but have different computational properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive occurrences requirement for LFP (Definition 3.10, Lemma 3.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: An occurrence of R in φ is positive if under an even number of negations. If φ is positive in R then the operator F_φ is monotone, guaranteeing a least fixed point and well-defined LFP semantics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing monotonicity is undecidable in general, so syntactic positivity is used as a safe restriction to ensure LFP is well-defined and has decidable syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive complexity correspondences (Theorems 3.13–3.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: ∃SO = NP (Fagin). Over finite ordered structures FO(LFP) = P (Immerman–Vardi). Over finite ordered structures FO(PFP) = PSPACE (Abiteboul–Vianu, Vardi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These theorems give machine-independent logical characterizations of complexity classes, central to linking logical fixed-point computations to computational complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-wise interpretation of fixed-point computations (Chapter 4 intuition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Least fixed point computations 'factor through' first-order computations: LFP's non-local influence at each stage is mediated by FO computations, which act as bottlenecks for information propagation in the induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to statistical mechanics: influences propagate via intermediate variables; this viewpoint underpins later connections between conditional independence/graphical factorization and polynomial-time computability.
